meta.chapterLabel: Lesson 2: Possession: Whose Pen Is This?

items.note: Used for physical objects ('this one'); to politely introduce a person, use こちら (kochira) instead.
Formed the same way as わたしの (watashino, 'my/mine'): [pronoun] + の (no) makes a possessive. Ask ownership with これはだれのですか (kore wa dare no desu ka), 'whose is this?'
The base question word this lesson's だれの (dareno, 'whose') is built from by adding の (no); used alone to ask who someone is.
A soft, humble way to say you don't know — often used to avoid a flat, direct refusal or when genuinely unsure.

の (no) attaches after わたし (watashi) to mean 'my' before a noun, as in the card for 'this is my pen,' or stands alone to mean 'mine,' as in the card for 'this is mine.' Same possessive の-pattern as だれの (dareno, 'whose').

items.reviewNote: Excluded as a duplicate: chapter-1 already teaches です with the gloss "To be (copula)". Same word, same meaning, glossed twice, which made the two cards an unanswerable Recognition collision. The earliest occurrence is kept.
items.note: The same です (desu) as the copula card from the earlier lesson; here it anchors a four-way paradigm with じゃありません (ja arimasen, negative), でした (deshita, past), and じゃありませんでした (ja arimasen deshita, past negative).
Negative form of です (desu); じゃ (ja) is more informal than では (dewa) but otherwise the same

items.target: これはとけいじゃありません
これはスミスさんのとけいです
items.note: Answers the だれの (dareno, 'whose') question by replacing だれ (dare) with a name: スミスさんの (Sumisu-san no), 'Smith-san's' — same [owner] の [thing] pattern as だれのですか (dare no desu ka).

items.target: これはわたしのペンです

items.note: Past-tense affirmative counterpart to です (desu) — 'was/were' instead of 'is/are.' Its negative partner is じゃありませんでした (ja arimasen deshita).

items.target: じゃありませんでした
items.note: Past negative form of です (desu); ではありませんでした (dewa arimasen deshita) is the less-informal equivalent

Same sound as the さん (san) title from Lesson 1 ('Mr., Mrs., Ms., Miss'), but an unrelated word. Position tells them apart: さん (san) after a person's name is the title, さん (san) in front of a counter is the number.

items.scene: counting, not a prefix or suffix

items.note: かいしゃ (kaisha, 'company') + の (no) + なまえ (namae, 'name') follows the same [owner] の [thing] pattern as の (no) itself — but not every noun pair links this way: でんわばんごう (denwa bangou, 'telephone number') just concatenates the two nouns directly, with no の (no) needed.
でんわ (denwa) means 'telephone' on its own; combines with ばんごう (bangou, 'number') to form でんわばんごう (denwa bangou, 'telephone number').
ばんごう (bangou) means 'number' on its own; combines with でんわ (denwa, 'telephone') to form でんわばんごう (denwa bangou, 'telephone number').
The everyday word for 'sweets'; it carries the honorific お (o) prefix attached to the front (お (o) + かし (kashi) → おかし (okashi)), and is the form you'll actually hear and say in conversation.

にほんの (nihon no) uses の (no) to turn 'Japan' into a modifier meaning 'from Japan / Japanese-made'; contrast にほんじん (nihonjin), which uses じん (jin) instead to mean 'a Japanese person' — の (no) describes a thing, じん (jin) names a person.
The bare phrase 'one more time'; add おねがいします (onegaishimasu) to turn it into a polite request — see もういちどおねがいします (mou ichido onegaishimasu).
Broader and a touch more polite/indirect than a plain request — can ask for an item, a service, or even a person, e.g. たなかさんをおねがいします (tanaka-san o onegaishimasu), 'may I speak with Tanaka-san'.
